name: Deepdweller (claude.ai)
note: Designed by Claude on claude.ai for the AI tournament, round 1 (won: 25.3 cells at day 3 against ChatGPT 2.7, Gemini 0). A long, swimmerless rod (radius 6, length 66) that steers only with a large buoyancy chamber. It uses its nitrogen sensor as a depth gauge: the chamber floats it whenever nitrogen reads 0.85 or more (about 1,250 µm deep or below), or whenever it is within ~45 µm of the floor, a wall or a crowd of kin while deeper than ~800 µm. Otherwise the chamber goes neutral and the cell sinks slowly, so it bobs just under the nutricline, where nitrogen (the real growth limit) is rich and light is still fine. It never goes shallow enough for light damage. The plastid is a 32%-of-body rod, so the cell earns more than its upkeep even lying on the floor. It stays awake all night so nitrogen uptake never drops to the resting rate. Starch plus oil (6.3M pJ, releasing about 26k pJ/s) cover a night of about 3.2M pJ, and the cell rests only as an emergency if its pool drops below 18%. On day 0 the floor reads nitrogen at about 1.0, so it pumps light and lifts off whatever way it lies, with a net lift of about 2.4 pN even with full stores. It has no divide rule, so it splits as soon as it has doubled, roughly twice a day while the water stays rich. Side spines keep attackers' tubes and mouths off its body, and its size makes it hard to swallow. Feeding tubes at each end drain any other species that drifts into them, for extra energy and nitrogen.

name: Deepdweller II (claude.ai)
note: Designed by Claude on claude.ai for the AI tournament, round 2 (its revision of Deepdweller). Refined round-1 winner. A slim, swimmerless rod (radius 5, length 72) that steers only with a big buoyancy chamber, using its nitrogen sensor as a depth gauge. It floats whenever nitrogen reads 0.85 or more (about 1,250 µm deep or below), or when within ~45 µm of the floor, a wall or kin while deeper than ~800 µm. Otherwise it sinks slowly, so it bobs just under the nutricline where nitrogen, the real limit on growth, is rich. The thinner body has about 19% more surface per volume than round 1's, so it takes up nitrogen faster and divides sooner. The plastid is 31% of the body, so it earns more than its upkeep even on the floor. It stays awake at night so it keeps taking up nitrogen at the full rate. Starch plus oil (3.7M pJ) cover a night of about 2.5M pJ and refill about 2.9M a day, and it rests only as an emergency. It lifts off the floor on day 0 whatever way it lies. Six side spines keep attackers' tubes and mouths off its body. Feeding tubes at both ends drain rival cells that touch them, and a small toxin sac leaks only while another species is within ~75 µm. Kin are immune, so copycats sharing its deep layer pay while it doesn't.

name: Gula (Claude, a swallower)
note: A swallower, retuned for the new balance (2026-11-04). A big rod 30 × 96 µm: a buoyancy chamber (22%) in front, a shade plastid (22%), an oil store (7%), the nucleus at the back; four mouths (front, back, two flanks). Its gape takes cells up to 7.5 µm in radius, and its free room (~30,000 µm³) holds a Deepdweller-sized rod: the slim tournament drifters are its food. Steered by light, not nitrogen (patchy nitrogen fools a nitrogen gauge): three eyespots; FLOATS when every eyespot sees less than 12% sun but one sees some (dim daylight: it rides ~1.2-1.5 mm by day), or when its feeler senses the floor within ~45 µm; at night its chamber goes neutral and it sinks to the nitrogen-rich floor, bouncing off it. RESTS when its energy is below 40%. Alone from the floor (3 runs, 5 days): never starving, 2 cells by day 5. In a 10-species contest it swallowed a Deepdweller once but was drained by the Deepdwellers' feeding tubes: big, rich and slow, it is a good meal.

name: Jaculella (Claude, a harpooner)
note: A harpooner, retuned for the new balance (2026-11-04): Gula's body (a rod 30 × 96 µm, chamber 22%, shade plastid 22%, oil 7%, steered by light, rests below 40% energy) with four 20 µm harpoons on its diagonal corners instead of mouths. Each fires when the feeler beside it feels another species within 20 µm, and more strongly than the feeler on the opposite corner (it shoots toward the side the stranger is on). Alone from the floor (3 runs, 5 days): never starving, 2-3 cells by day 5. In a 10-species contest it threw 23 harpoons, hit twice and killed a Raptilla 2, but was drained by the Deepdwellers.

name: Leviathella (Claude, a giant hunter)
note: A predator giant (author, 2026-11-04: "big predators that eat prey"; Noctiluca-like): a rod 100 × 300 µm (radius 50, length 200), 2 µm plates (harpoon wounds ÷5), eight mouths round its body. Its gape takes any cell up to 25 µm in radius, and its free room (~1 million µm³) holds almost anything: every species in the tank is food, and each meal gives half the prey's nitrogen, which a giant lacks to divide. Inside: a buoyancy chamber (22%), a shade plastid (22%), oil (7%), the nucleus; steered by light like Pachyderma (dim daylight floats it; nights on the floor), rests below 40% energy. Alone from the floor (3 runs, 5 days): never starving, 1.1× in 5 days.

name: Miasmella (Claude, toxic)
note: Toxic, retuned for the new balance (2026-11-04): Gula's body lengthened to 30 × 108 µm (chamber 22%, shade plastid 22%, oil 7%, steered by light, rests below 40% energy) with a toxin sac (radius 4) of Kind Leak between the plastid and the oil, leaking all the time: a cloud that drifts round it and harms other species (energy and plastids); kin are immune. Alone from the floor (3 runs, 5 days): never starving, 2 cells by day 5. In a 10-species contest it killed nobody (currents carry a lone cell's cloud off) and was drained by the Deepdwellers.

name: Noctilla (Claude)
note: A swimmer that survives day and night from the floor, no buoyancy chamber. Round, 20 µm, a 48 µm pulling tail at the front, three eyespots (front, left, right) so one always looks up even lying on the floor. The tail runs while ALL eyespots see less than 25% sun (deep, dim: climb); in brighter light it stops and slowly sinks, so by day it holds ~950 µm. It rests when ALL eyespots see less than 1% (night): flagella stop and it sinks, from ~300 µm at dusk to ~1.3 mm by dawn, away from the surface. Measured from the floor, any way up: 3 days, never starving, pool never below 30%.

name: Pachyderma (Claude, a giant)
note: A passive giant, the elephant (author, 2026-11-04: "big animals like elephants, that are more passive"): the biggest body the game allows, a rod 100 × 300 µm (radius 50, length 200), 2.1 million µm³. Armoured: 5 µm cellulose plates (thick walls are allowed on big cells: a harpoon wound ÷11, a feeding tube pays ×11 to pierce) and 20 spines 30 µm long along its flanks and corners (they catch harpoon darts and keep tubes and mouths off). Inside: a buoyancy chamber (22%), a shade plastid (22%), oil (7%), the nucleus; steered by light (floats in dim daylight, riding ~1.4 mm by day; sinks to the floor at night and bounces off it), rests below 40% energy. Alone from the floor (3 runs, 5 days): never starving, but it grows only 1.1× in 5 days: nitrogen comes in through the surface and a giant has little surface for its volume. Nearly immortal, nearly sterile.

name: Plebella (Claude, a swarm)
note: A swarm that wins by numbers (the author's strategy, 2026-11-04: very small, explosive growth, short lives, toxins, sticking to the enemy). A tiny rod 8 × 32 µm with NO nucleus: no rules and no brain upkeep, so every part runs all the time and it divides the moment it has doubled. A shade plastid (30%, made for dim water), an oil store (12%) to carry the night, a toxin sac of Kind Leak that always leaks (kin are immune), four mucus pads on its flanks that grab any other cell they touch, and kin pads at both tips so daughters chain end to end. It lives low, near the nitrogen-rich floor. Alone from the floor: 32 cells by day 3.5, no deaths. Against one Deepdweller (3 runs, 5 days): won one outright (both Deepdwellers poisoned by day 2.9, then 60 Plebellas), lost cells to the Deepdweller's feeding tubes in the others (it drains them: 40k pJ to pierce for a small meal). Against Deepdweller II: weakened it but never took over (2-12 cells). Weaknesses: no brain, so it can't time its divisions; feeding tubes pick it off before its boom.

name: Raptilla (Claude, a hunter)
note: A hunter (a mixotroph, like Dinophysis): Noctilla's body (round, 20 µm, a 48 µm pulling tail at the front, three eyespots, two plastids, an oil store) plus a 20 µm peduncle beside the tail, angled 20° forward, so prey it swims past slides along the tube. It lives on light like Noctilla (climbs while all eyespots see less than 25% sun, rests in the dark) and feeds on any other species it touches. Its tail STOPS WHILE FEEDING (the built-in Feeding reading): without that its own pull tore every latch off within a third of a second (27 latches on Saltella in 2 minutes, 40k each, ~2k kept). With it: one latch held 218 s, drained 1.8 million pJ (kept half) and killed the Saltella. Meetings are rare: in 2 days it met only Saltella, at a shared depth.

name: Raptilla 2 (Claude, a thief)
note: Raptilla grown up: the same hunter (Noctilla's body, a 20 µm peduncle beside its pulling tail, the tail stops while feeding), with two rules changed: it DIVIDES only once its Size is more than 3× (so it has room for stolen plastids), and it FEEDS only while any eyespot sees more than 5% sun (so a heavy prey can't drag it down to the floor in the dark). In the contest with stealing it farmed its prey: 26 latches, only 3 kills, six thieves by day 10, one at 2.7× carrying 4 stolen plastids.

name: Saltella (Claude, a jumper)
note: No tail, no chamber: it travels by jumping. Two springs at the back, mirror copies of each other (one spring alone curves every jump ~26° to one side and turned it upside down within a few hops; the pair cancels). They fire when NO eyespot sees more than 15% sun AND at least one sees more than 1.5%: the cell sinks slowly, and every time the light gets too dim it hops 200-400 µm up; about 10 jumps a day. A 60 µm spine in front keeps it front-up as it sinks (the springs drag like a shuttlecock's feathers and tipped it front-down without it). Rests when all eyespots see less than 1%. Its day: dawn, 2-4 jumps from the depths to ~400 µm; then it drifts down all day (~1.3 mm by mid-afternoon) and hops back; at dusk it chases the fading light to the top, then rests and sinks to ~1.6 mm by dawn. Measured from the floor: 3 days, never starving, starch full by late morning. Weakness: dropped on the floor with its front pointing below level it is stuck (jumps only slide it along the floor) and starves; in its normal life it always lands front-up. UPDATE (2026-11-02): its springs also fire while it is being drained ("or when it is being drained"): a jump tears a hunter's tube off (the tube snaps under a sustained pull) and throws it ~1 mm away; before, a latched Saltella sat drained for minutes.

name: Trochilla (Claude, the cartwheel)
note: The author's idea: oars all round and statoliths to steer. Round, 20 µm; four 40 µm flexible oars in a plus (front, back, left, right); two small statoliths at right angles (one faces the front, one the left: together they know which way up the cell is; one alone can't tell left from right); four eyespots on the diagonals. Each oar rows only while it points within ~80° of DOWN (its statolith above 60% or below 40%), so whatever way up the cell is, the oars underneath push it up: it has no right way up and climbs from the floor lying any way (Saltella can't). Each stroke twists the body, so it doesn't swim straight: it cartwheels (~20°/s), handing the job from oar to oar. Oars row while no eyespot sees more than 25% sun and one sees more than 1.5%; it rests when all see less than 1%. Its day: rolls up from the depths at dawn (~9 µm/s), rides 700-900 µm, chases the dusk light to ~400 µm, rests and sinks to ~1.7 mm by dawn (off the surface at night). Measured from the floor at any angle: 3 days, never starving, starch full by mid-afternoon. Uses 11 brain slots (needs the 16-slot nucleus).
